strengths: The paper poses a clear and interesting problem: adding reusable procedural skills to frozen LLMs while preserving compositionality. The three desired properties P1-P3 make the objective concrete and help structure the evaluation.

The proposed skill-centered training setup is conceptually sensible, and the controlled digit-transformation environment gives explicit skill labels, exact train/test composition splits, and unambiguous accuracy metrics.

The experiments provide evidence that placing learned soft tokens at semantically relevant operation positions can improve OOD skill composition over LoRA and standard prefix-style prompt tuning in this synthetic setting.

The ablations on token length, training composition complexity, and initialization are useful and reveal nontrivial behavior, especially the apparent capacity/generalization tradeoff for soft skill tokens.

The paper is generally readable, includes substantial experimental details, and has an honest limitations section acknowledging the proof-of-concept nature, dataset construction challenge, and soft-token optimization issues.
weaknesses: The central claims about scalable skill-based continual learning are much stronger than the evidence. The main evaluation is limited to two new synthetic digit-sequence operations on a Qwen2.5-0.5B model that was itself LoRA-trained on the synthetic operation language. This does not demonstrate applicability to realistic LLM skills or natural language tasks.

The distinction between skill neologisms and prompt tuning is not fully isolated. The proposed method replaces the target operation token with learned soft tokens at the relevant location, while the prompt-tuning baseline uses a prefix. Thus the gains may come from insertion position or prompt format rather than vocabulary-level integration or a qualitatively new neologism mechanism.

Baselines are incomplete for the main claim. Important comparisons would include soft tokens inserted at the operation position without framing them as vocabulary extensions, learned embeddings for discrete new operation tokens, prefix/prompt tuning with matched semantic placement, and stronger compositional prompt/adaptor baselines. The claim that existing PEFT/prefix approaches are structurally unable to satisfy P3 is overstated without testing composable prompt/adaptor variants.

The pretrained-skill-token motivation in Section 4 is weak. The XOR/XNOR keyword experiment has only 100 samples, few prompts, no controls for token frequency versus semantic prior, and does not convincingly show that vocabulary tokens encode procedural knowledge rather than simply cueing a memorized/common task.

The reported results are mixed and sometimes modest. For 3-skill OOD composition, skill neologisms average around 0.65-0.70 accuracy, with high variance in several tables. Zero-shot composition degrades with sequence length, and the strongest conclusions are phrased more definitively than the data warrant.

Reproducibility is only partial. Hyperparameters and dataset generation details are given, but there is no clear code release, seed reporting, statistical testing, or enough detail to verify implementation choices such as tokenizer extension, loss masking, decoding/evaluation parsing, or exact prompt formats for all methods.

The setup weakens the continual-learning framing: the base model is first specialized to a synthetic algebra of operations, REV fails to generalize and is removed from held-out tests, and only two new skills are added. This is far from demonstrating continual accumulation of many independent skills.

Presentation has several imprecisions and overclaims, such as treating no weight updates as preventing catastrophic forgetting in general, asserting prefix methods cannot compose independently without a sufficiently broad comparison, and using 'skill neologism' terminology for what may be semantically placed soft prompts. Ethical risks are minimal for this toy setting, but the paper does not discuss risks of adding opaque learned capabilities to deployed LLMs.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear and relevant problem: adding new model capabilities without updating the base weights, while preserving compositional use with existing skills. The three desired properties P1-P3 are useful framing for skill-based continual learning.

The core idea of learning skill-specific soft tokens at the vocabulary/input-embedding level is plausible and connects several lines of work: prompt tuning, neologisms, tool tokens, and compositional skill evaluation.

The controlled digit-sequence experiments are cleanly defined, with explicit skill labels, held-out skill combinations, and several ablations on token length, training composition complexity, and initialization. The appendix gives many implementation details and hyperparameters, which helps reproducibility.
The limitations section is unusually candid about the proof-of-concept nature of the work, the dependence on skill-centered datasets, soft-token optimization instability, and computational costs.
weaknesses: The central claims are not adequately supported. The experiments are almost entirely on a narrow synthetic digit-transformation domain with only two learned skills, so the paper does not convincingly demonstrate a scalable path to skill-based continual learning for LLMs in realistic settings.

The comparison to prompt tuning is not fully fair or diagnostic. Skill neologisms replace the operation token at the semantically relevant location, while the prompt-tuning baseline uses a prefix. The observed gains may therefore come from insertion position and task formatting rather than vocabulary-level integration or a genuinely new mechanism.

The paper overclaims P3 and the contrast with existing methods. It states that LoRA or prefix-style methods are structurally unable to compose independently trained skills, but there is prior work on adapter composition, prompt composition, routing, merging, and multi-adapter inference. These baselines are not tested.

The Section 4 evidence that pretrained LLMs contain procedural skill tokens is weak. The XOR/XNOR experiment uses only 100 examples and prompt variants that confound keyword familiarity, instruction wording, and in-context learning. It does not establish that a token encodes procedural knowledge rather than simply triggering a familiar task distribution.

The work does not actually evaluate continual learning in the usual sense. There is no sequential addition of many skills, no growing library of neologisms, no interference analysis among many learned tokens, and no comparison of memory/compute tradeoffs at scale. P1 is true only by construction, not empirically connected to a broader continual-learning scenario.

The base model is itself specially trained on synthetic operations before learning neologisms, which weakens the claim that the method extends modern pretrained LLMs. The approach may rely heavily on the constructed pretraining environment and explicit bracketed operation grammar.

Results are mixed and sometimes fragile: OOD accuracy varies substantially by held-out skill, 3-skill performance remains modest, random initialization can degrade performance, and longer token lengths collapse in some settings. These issues are acknowledged but not resolved.

Presentation is generally readable, but several claims are stronger than the evidence warrants, and there are minor writing/formatting issues. More importantly, the paper does not provide enough evidence on code/data release or exact reproducibility beyond hyperparameter tables.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear and useful problem: adding new procedural skills to frozen LLMs while preserving compositionality. The three desiderata P1-P3 are well motivated and make the contribution easy to evaluate.

The proposed skill neologism mechanism is simple and technically plausible: vocabulary-integrated soft tokens trained on skill-centered data, with model weights frozen. The distinction from ordinary prompt tuning is empirically probed rather than only asserted.

The controlled digit-transformation benchmark is well suited to isolating compositional transfer. The ID/OOD skill splits, held-out skills, independently trained skill composition experiment, and ablations over token length, training composition complexity, and initialization provide meaningful evidence for the central proof of concept.

Results are encouraging: skill neologisms outperform LoRA and prompt tuning on OOD combinations in the synthetic setup, and independently learned SHIFT and INV-POL neologisms compose better than an in-context learning baseline.

The paper is generally well organized, with useful appendices giving hyperparameters, dataset construction, evaluation details, and resource information. The limitations section is honest about the controlled nature of the experiments, skill-centered dataset requirements, soft-token instability, and compute cost.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is narrow. The main evidence comes from a single synthetic digit-sequence environment and a Qwen2.5-0.5B model adapted to that environment. This supports a proof of concept but not yet the broader claims about scalable skill-based continual learning in realistic LLM settings.

The method relies on skill-centered datasets where the target skill is explicitly identifiable and inserted in a semantically natural position. The paper argues such datasets may be obtainable with LLM annotation or existing labels, but provides no experiment on natural language, code, math, tool use, or another less controlled domain where skill boundaries are noisy.

The comparison to prompt tuning may not fully isolate the important factor. Skill neologisms differ from prefix prompt tuning mainly by insertion location and vocabulary-style integration, but the paper does not compare to stronger or more flexible soft-token baselines such as operation-position soft prompts, multiple learned prompt tokens inserted at the skill location without vocabulary framing, prefix-tuning at deeper layers, prompt ensembling/mixtures, or adapter-composition methods.

The base model is itself trained on the synthetic operation language, so the experiments test adding two nearby operations to an already specialized model. It remains unclear whether the approach can learn skills that are less structurally homologous to the pretraining operations or that require new algorithmic circuits rather than recombining existing ones.

Some quantitative results show substantial residual weakness: OOD performance varies by held-out skill and new skill, 3-skill composition is only moderate, and random initialization can be unstable. These results are compatible with the paper's limitations, but they temper the strength of the central claim.

The Section 4 evidence that pretrained tokens encode procedural knowledge is suggestive but not decisive. The XOR/XNOR keyword experiment may conflate token familiarity, prompt prior, and operation knowledge, and uses only 100 examples per setting with no deeper controls over tokenization, frequency, or alternative keywords.

Reproducibility is decent at the hyperparameter level, but the manuscript does not clearly state whether code, data-generation scripts, trained neologisms, or evaluation scripts will be released. For a synthetic benchmark, exact release would be important for reliable comparison.

Presentation is mostly clear, but there are several grammatical and formatting issues, and some claims in Table 1 and the discussion are stronger than the evidence warrants, especially the categorical assertion that prefix-based methods cannot support multi-skill composition without considering recent compositional prompt/adaptor variants. Ethical risks appear limited, but there is no explicit ethics discussion beyond technical limitations.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and interesting formulation of skill-based continual learning, with explicit desiderata for no base-model weight updates, OOD compositional transfer, and zero-shot composition of independently learned skills.

The core idea of treating learned soft tokens as vocabulary-level skill neologisms is simple, technically plausible, and meaningfully distinct from standard task-level prompt tuning when the tokens are inserted at semantically relevant positions.

The synthetic digit-transformation benchmark is well chosen for isolating compositionality: skills, compositions, held-out skills, and exact-match evaluation are all unambiguous, which makes the main mechanistic claims easier to interpret.

The empirical comparisons against LoRA and prompt tuning show a consistent advantage for skill neologisms on held-out skill compositions, while the ablations on token length, composition complexity, initialization, and label noise provide useful insight into when the method works.

The paper includes substantial experimental detail in the appendix, including prompts, hyperparameters, dataset construction, and evaluation settings, and the limitations section is honest about dependence on skill-centered data and soft-token optimization instability.
weaknesses: The main evidence is still narrow relative to the broad framing of scalable continual learning. Most convincing results come from a highly synthetic environment where the base model is itself trained on symbolic operation tokens and where the new skills are close variants of existing sequence transformations.

The natural-language validation is quite small: only two target skills, 300 generated training examples per skill, and 50 test queries, with GPT-5 both generating training answers and grading outputs. This is a useful proof of concept but not enough to establish broad applicability to realistic fuzzy skills.

The claim of learning without weight updates is slightly overstated. The base model weights are frozen, but the method adds and optimizes new embedding parameters and extends the tokenizer/vocabulary; this is parameter growth and deployment complexity rather than purely context-only learning.

The comparison to prompt tuning is not fully controlled. Skill neologisms differ not only by vocabulary integration but also by semantically targeted insertion/replacement locations, while the prompt-tuning baseline uses a prefix. The experiments therefore do not cleanly isolate whether vocabulary-level integration, insertion position, or prompt semantics drives the gains.

The P3 comparison is somewhat limited because LoRA and standard prompt tuning are treated as structurally unable to compose, so the main zero-shot composition comparison is against ICL only. More relevant baselines could include composable adapters, multitask soft-prompt methods, or jointly trained upper bounds for the two new skills.

Some empirical results are mixed or fragile: the pretrained synthetic model has poor generalization for REV and decreasing performance for longer sequence lengths; OOD results vary substantially by held-out skill; and the length ablation shows that larger soft-token capacity can collapse OOD performance.

Reproducibility is incomplete as written: the manuscript states that code can be found at blank locations, and the Skill-Mix experiment relies on GPT-5 generation and grading, which may be difficult to reproduce exactly without fixed artifacts or API/model-version details.

The impact statement is too cursory. A method for adding latent capabilities through opaque soft tokens raises safety, auditability, and misuse concerns, especially because the learned tokens are not human-interpretable; these issues deserve more concrete discussion and evaluation.

strengths: The paper has a clear motivating idea: treat learned soft vocabulary tokens as reusable skill handles, trained on skill-centered data, and test whether they compose with held-out skills and with each other.
The controlled digit-transformation setup is well aligned with the paper's main mechanistic question because skills and compositions are explicit, allowing clean ID/OOD splits.

The paper includes useful ablations on token length, composition complexity, initialization, and label noise, and the results show some nontrivial behavior, especially the capacity/generalization tradeoff.
The limitations section is fairly candid about dependence on skill-centered datasets, soft-token instability, and training cost.
weaknesses: The central claim that skill neologisms provide a scalable path toward skill-based continual learning is not supported by the evidence. Most results are on a highly synthetic digit task with only two new skills, and the natural-language validation uses only two selected Skill-Mix skills, 300 generated examples per skill, and 50 test queries.

The comparison to prompt tuning and LoRA is not fully convincing. The paper argues that LoRA/prompt tuning are structurally unable to satisfy multi-skill composition, but does not evaluate stronger compositional PEFT baselines such as adapter arithmetic/merging, multitask prompt mixtures, shared/task-specific prompts, or simple joint training upper bounds.

The Section 4 evidence for existing procedural tokens is weak. The XOR/XNOR experiment uses only 100 examples, 3-bit strings, and prompt variants that confound token familiarity, instruction following, and task naming; it does not establish that individual vocabulary embeddings encode reusable procedural knowledge.

The Skill-Mix experiment is underpowered and fragile: it uses GPT-5 both to generate training data and grade outputs, reports no confidence intervals or human validation, selects skills where the base model is weak, and evaluates only one pair of target skills. This is too little evidence for broad natural-language applicability.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript contains blank code links, relies on proprietary GPT-5 generation/grading, and omits enough implementation detail to make exact replication difficult despite some hyperparameter tables.

The base model in the synthetic experiments is itself LoRA-trained on the same artificial operation language before the proposed method is evaluated, making the setup closer to a custom toy environment than evidence about pretrained LLM continual learning.

The presentation overstates conclusions. Terms like “skill-based continual learning,” “procedural knowledge,” and “vocabulary-level integration” are used ambitiously, but the experiments do not show long-horizon continual addition, retention across many skills, scaling to realistic model sizes, or robustness to ambiguous real-world skill definitions.

Some experimental choices reduce confidence: REV is excluded after poor generalization, OOD performance remains uneven for several held-out operations, and the paper does not provide statistical tests across seeds for the main comparisons.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful framing for skill-based continual learning, with three concrete desiderata: no weight updates, compositional transfer, and zero-shot multi-skill composition.

The central idea of training skill-specific soft vocabulary tokens on skill-centered datasets is simple, well-motivated, and potentially valuable; the distinction from ordinary task-level prompt tuning is explained clearly.

The controlled digit-sequence experiments are thoughtfully designed, with explicit skill definitions, held-out skills, ID/OOD composition splits, LoRA and prompt-tuning baselines, and ablations over token length, training composition complexity, initialization, and label noise.

Results support the main proof-of-concept: skill neologisms outperform LoRA and prompt tuning on held-out synthetic skill compositions, and independently learned skill tokens can be combined zero-shot better than an ICL baseline.
The paper is generally well written and includes a candid limitations section covering skill-centered dataset availability, soft-token instability, and computational cost.
weaknesses: The evidence remains preliminary relative to the broad continual-learning claims. Most of the empirical support comes from a highly controlled synthetic transformation environment with a specially adapted Qwen2.5-0.5B base model, so it is unclear how well the method scales to open-ended skills in ordinary pretrained LLMs.

The natural-language validation is promising but narrow: only two Skill-Mix target skills, 300 training examples per skill, 50 joint test queries, one small instruct model, GPT-5-generated training data, and GPT-5 grading. This makes the external validity and statistical reliability limited.

Some comparisons are not fully satisfying. LoRA and standard prompt tuning are not designed for post-hoc composition, but stronger baselines such as adapter composition, multitask prompt tuning, learned prompt mixtures, or jointly trained soft-token variants would better isolate the benefit of vocabulary-level skill tokens.

The claimed advantage over prompt tuning is partly confounded by insertion position and replacement semantics: skill neologisms replace skill tokens at semantically relevant locations, whereas the prompt-tuning baseline uses a prefix. More controlled variants would strengthen the causal claim that vocabulary integration itself is decisive.

The Section 4 evidence that existing tokens encode procedural knowledge is suggestive but weak: XOR/XNOR with 100 samples and three examples may reflect memorized task naming or prompt effects rather than a general phenomenon of vocabulary-level procedural skill storage.

Reproducibility is only partial from the manuscript. The appendices give many useful hyperparameters, but the code link appears blank/redacted in the extracted manuscript, and it is not clear whether generated Skill-Mix data, prompts, seeds, and GPT-5 grader outputs will be released.

The impact statement is minimal. While the method is not obviously high-risk, improving modular capability acquisition in LLMs has dual-use implications and safety interactions that deserve more concrete discussion than saying no specific consequences are identified.
